why: Repository audits show hierarchy/dynamic-outline gains confounded by read amplification; accuracy branch shows complex trace architecture can still miss the decisive inference. Test retrieval, selection, verification, coordination, and simplicity as rival bottlenecks under matched cost.

Primary benchmark paper that explicitly disentangles retrieval quality, search count, and model reasoning on a fixed human-verified corpus; directly tests whether retrieval can dominate architecture.
Direct primary ablation of text-ranking components in deep research; isolates retrieval unit, first-stage ranker, reranker, query formulation, end-to-end accuracy, and search-call cost.
Peer-reviewed primary trace study across seven multi-agent systems and 200 annotated traces; directly measures coordination and compliance failure classes rather than assuming decomposition helps.

Primary equal-thinking-token comparison across single-agent and multiple coordination architectures; closest available causal test of whether hierarchy itself beats a simpler workflow at matched compute.

Strongest available primary operational counterexample: production deep-research system reporting a multi-agent win, plus its own cost attribution and failure lessons; needed to state what hierarchy actually survives.

Primary controlled study designed to separate retrieval failure from long-context utilization; directly tests whether handing an agent more trace/output can lower performance despite perfect evidence availability.

Strongest controlled evidence favoring dynamic outlines and hierarchical section synthesis; needed as decisive disconfirmation and to isolate whether gains come from hierarchy or focused evidence addressing.

Independent primary controlled study of 180 agent configurations across architectures, models, and task structure; tests when coordination helps or reverses rather than assuming a universal hierarchy gain.
Primary adaptive-retrieval controller study with error analysis; directly tests stopping/sufficiency and whether extra retrieval is monotonically beneficial.

decision: Saturation reached after 9 completed rounds, 11 manifests, 207 retrieved candidates, 9 selected primaries/operational sources, and 7 uncapped rereads; stop on claim saturation, not the unlimited budget.
why: Round 8 independently confirmed task-conditional coordination and overhead under matched compute; round 9 added non-monotonic iteration and failure-distribution evidence but no new bottleneck class. Top ordering is stable across local A/Bs and distinct external origins.
